extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics; readers of Kant
extracted.subtask_description: The text gives philosophical criteria for judging beauty, distinguishing kinds of artistic production, and defining genius versus taste; it explains what makes judgments of taste 'pure', how art relates to nature, and what conditions artistic genius. Useful for evaluating or producing aesthetic works according to Kantian theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as sensus communis / faculty of judging universal communicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste can be called 'sensus communis' — the faculty of judging that which makes universally communicable, without the mediation of a concept; taste is the faculty of judging a priori of the communicability of feelings bound up with a given representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste arises when imagination in its freedom awakens the understanding and plays together without aid of concepts, producing a feeling that is communicable. The judgement of taste concerns the feeling of pleasure and its universal communicability rather than cognitive concepts. (See also relation between imagination and understanding; requirement that judgement be 'a priori'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness of the pure judgement of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste, by which something is declared beautiful, must have no interest as its determining ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although empirical or intellectual interests may be combined with a pure aesthetic judgement indirectly (e.g., pleasure in the object's existence), they must not determine it. A 'pure' aesthetic judgement is distinguished by being free from ulterior motives or desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical interest in the Beautiful (social/sociability interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirically the Beautiful interests only in society: taste is a faculty for judging things in respect of which we can communicate our feeling to all other men; it furthers what everyone's natural inclination (sociability) desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains adornment and cultivation of beauty as social phenomena (e.g., ornaments, forms in canoes, clothes) and shows how universal communicability increases worth. But this empirical interest is subordinate to 'pure' taste and may conflate pleasant with good; it gives an ambiguous transition from the Pleasant to the Good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual (moral-like) interest in the Beautiful of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: An immediate intellectual interest in the beauty of Nature (not merely judgement of it) is a mark of a good soul and indicates a disposition favourable to moral feeling when bound to contemplation of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interest is immediate only when one takes pleasure in the mere presence of natural beauty (not its charms or use). Deception (artificial substitutes posing as nature) destroys the immediate interest. Thus natural beauty has a privileged status: it arouses an interest akin to moral feeling because it appears purposive in a way that points to our moral destination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Art and Nature (Art = production through freedom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is distinguished from Nature as doing (facere) is distinguished from acting/working generally (agere); art is properly production through freedom, i.e., through a will that places Reason at the basis of its actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Products lacking rational deliberation (e.g., bee cells) are analogically called art but are natural/instinctive. Art presupposes a representation in the cause prior to actuality. Art also differs from science (practical vs theoretical) and from handicraft (free vs mercenary). Even 'free' art requires mechanism/rules (e.g., prosody in poetry); removing constraints does not necessarily produce free art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasant arts vs Beautiful (aesthetical) arts — purpose determines class
rubrics_metrics.description: If an art's immediate design is mere pleasure (sensation) it is 'pleasant' art; if its immediate design is the feeling of pleasure derived from modes of cognition (reflective judgement) it is 'beautiful' (aesthetical) art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: convivial storytelling, table arrangement, music for gaiety, and games that merely entertain are pleasant arts. Beautiful art is purposive for itself and furthers the culture of mental powers in reference to social communication; its standard is reflective judgement, not sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful art must 'look like nature' (purposiveness without apparent design)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a product of beautiful art we must be conscious it is Art yet feel the purposiveness of its form as if it were free from constraint — i.e., it must 'look' like Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although art observes the rules punctiliously, these rules should not painfully obtrude; the form of schools should not show. If the design appears obviously deliberate (aiming only at sensation or a definite object), it pleases by sensation or concept and is mechanical rather than beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as the innate talent that gives the rule to Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is the innate productive faculty (ingenium) through which Nature gives the rule to Art; it is the talent for producing what no definite rule can prescribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties of genius: (1) originality (cannot be reduced to rule), (2) exemplarity (products serve as models), (3) incommunicable method (the author cannot set out how Ideas arise), (4) nature gives the rule to Art not Science. Genius is opposed to imitation/teachability; models of genius transmit ideas by example rather than precept. Nevertheless every beautiful art has a mechanical element that rules execution and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of faculties: taste judges, genius produces
rubrics_metrics.description: For judging beautiful objects as such, taste is requisite; for producing beautiful art, genius is requisite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural beauty (a thing) requires taste to judge; artificial beauty (a representation) requires accounting for the object's intended purpose and presupposes genius for its production. Thus competence to evaluate is distinct from the capacity to create.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judging artificial beauty must consider concept/purpose (perfection of the thing)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the object is given as a product of art, and as such to be declared beautiful, there must be, at bottom, a concept of what the thing is to be; perfection with respect to its purpose must be taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural beauty can be judged without a concept of purpose; artificial beauty is judged with respect to teleological considerations (the object's intended end). When we judge living natural objects aesthetically by reference to purposes, the judgement is no longer purely aesthetical but teleological-aesthetical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of artistic representation: disgust cannot be made beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one kind of ugliness which cannot be represented in accordance with nature without destroying all aesthetical satisfaction and consequently artificial beauty: that which excites disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other calamitous or 'ugly' subjects (the Furies, war, disease) can be represented as beautiful; but 'disgust' intrudes upon imagination such that artistic representation cannot distance it into a pleasurable judgement. Sculpture, because its products almost interchange with nature, avoids direct representation of disgust and uses allegory/attributes to represent such themes indirectly.
